title: The future of the notwithstanding clause is now up to political leaders
summary: The task of governing the use of the notwithstanding clause has been left to the players in the political arena. If invoking the clause is to become politically difficult again, it will be up to…

image.caption: The Supreme Court ruled on Friday that Quebec's secularism law, which pre-emptively used the notwithstanding clause to temporarily override certain Charter rights, was largely valid. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Two weeks after he pieced together the "kitchen accord," Jean Chrétien stood in the House of Commons as justice minister to present a new constitutional resolution, including a Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
In his remarks on that momentous occasion, Chrétien made a specific effort to defend the presence in the Charter of an "override" clause.

"The effect of this provision is, first, that it will be politically very difficult for a government to introduce without very good reason a measure which applies notwithstanding the Charter of Rights and Freedoms in the Constitution," he said on the afternoon of Nov. 20, 1981.

blocks.text: Chrétien quoted a prominent lawyer — Alan Borovoy, the general counsel for the Canadian Civil Liberties Association — who said the notwithstanding clause would be a "red flag for opposition parties and the press."
"This will make it politically difficult for a government to override the Charter," Chrétien quoted Borovoy as saying. "Political difficulty is a reasonable safeguard for the Charter."

Forty-five years and one week later, amid growing concern that the clause is now being invoked too easily and too casually by governments and legislatures to pass laws that would otherwise be found to violate the rights of Canadians, the Supreme Court of Canada delivered a landmark ruling on the political compromise of 1981.

The court upheld the Quebec legislature's use of the clause in the case of Bill 21 and it did not find that there should be new limits on how the clause can be used. A majority of justices did find that the invocation of the clause does not prevent a court from publicly declaring that the rights of Canadians are being violated — a measure that may, in future, make it somewhat harder for governments to do so.

But the larger task of governing the use of the notwithstanding clause has been left to the players in the political arena. If the notwithstanding clause is to become politically difficult again, it will be up to political actors.
'The courts have a crucial role to play'

The question of whether courts might provide "declaratory relief" — a judicial declaration on whether rights have been unreasonably infringed, but without invalidating the law in question — even after the notwithstanding clause has been invoked had split the governments that filed arguments with the Supreme Court.

The federal government as well as the governments of Manitoba and British Columbia thought it permissible and potentially useful. Ontario, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Quebec were opposed (Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon reiterated his province's opposition to declaratory relief on Friday).
The seven justices of the Supreme Court were also split, but with the majority in favour.

"The five-year expiry period set out in [the notwithstanding clause], which corresponds to the maximum duration of the House of Commons or a legislative assembly under s. 4 of the Charter, is clearly intended to place in the hands of the electorate the choice of whether to renew the override provision," Justice Nicholas Kasirer wrote in Friday's ruling.
"Furthermore, the court's opinion is useful for the public, particularly where a vulnerable minority is affected by an overriding statute."
'A full attack on Charter rights': Critics warn of fallout from Bill 21 ruling

Justices Andromache Karakatsanis and Michelle O'Bonsawin concurred that, "courts have a crucial role to play in dialogue between the legislatures and electorate by informing both of the scope of a Charter right and whether and to what extent it is infringed by a statute that invokes the notwithstanding clause."

That courts can offer comment even after the notwithstanding clause has been invoked also goes some way toward answering concerns about recent "pre-emptive" uses of the clause — when governments invoke the clause even before a court has had a chance to pass judgment on the law.

"The court confirmed that Canadians have the right to know when their Charter rights have been unjustifiably infringed when the notwithstanding clause has been invoked," Sean Fraser, the federal justice minister, said in a statement on Friday. "This is an important part of ensuring transparency, accountability and a healthy democracy."
That may be of limited solace to those whose rights are in question. But it points back to the political arena.
The price of liberty?

Even if one disagrees with all previous uses of the clause there might still be a case for what Chrétien called a "safety valve" (one of those who pushed for the clause was Allan Blakeney, the NDP premier of Saskatchewan). And even critics of the clause might need to wrestle with arguments that there could be significant downsides to doing away with it — that, in the absence of a notwithstanding clause, courts might only become more politicized, with political leaders more incentivized to appoint judges who will decide a certain way (as it is in the United States).

A future court may some day decide that a particular use of the notwithstanding clause has gone too far (in Friday's ruling, three justices seemed to allow that there could be some theoretical outer limits). For now, the options for outright overriding the override may be limited to either the difficult (constitutional negotiations to amend the Charter) or the dangerous (reviving the federal Parliament's power to disallow provincial laws).
If the court had ruled on Friday that there were significant legal limits on the use of clause, the result could have been a constitutional crisis.

At the federal level — where the notwithstanding clause has never been invoked — Sen. Peter Harder has proposed a bill that would at least establish new rules and requirements around any use of the clause by Parliament. Under Harder's bill, for instance, the support of two-thirds of MPs would be required to invoke the clause.
It would, in other words, make it somewhat more difficult to invoke the clause.

Eugene Forsey, the late senator and constitutional scholar, once colourfully described the notwithstanding clause as a "dagger pointed at the heart of our fundamental freedoms." One might agree with that sentiment and yet still agree with Roy McMurtry, the attorney general of Ontario in 1981, who said that "political accountability is the best safeguard against any improper use of the 'override clause.'"

If it has become too easy to invoke the notwithstanding clause in recent years, it is still likely not for the court to rewrite the Charter — to change the result of a compromise brokered by political actors. Rather, it suggests that political accountability has been lacking.
"For those who remain concerned about the override clause, let me remind them that it has been said that the price of liberty is eternal vigilance," Chrétien told the House in November 1981.
It is actually unclear who, if anyone, ever actually said that. But the sentiment might still be worthy.

"Pressure groups must remain vigilant," Chrétien said, commending the "vigilance" of women who were then pushing for Section 28 of the Charter, on gender rights, to be excluded from the notwithstanding clause. (On Friday, the Court found Section 28 did not invalidate Bill 21.)
Vigilance may not be the most satisfying answer. But it might be the best or only one available.
